Spouse
spous
n. (a betrothed or wedded companion; in the Song, the bride — Hebrew kallah)
Latin sponsa, a betrothed woman, from spondere, to promise solemnly. The Hebrew kallah means bride or daughter-in-law — a woman brought into a house by covenant.

Biblical Definition

Spouse in the Authorized Version belongs almost entirely to the Song of Solomon, where the bridegroom uses it repeatedly and never without an endearment attached. “Come with me from Lebanon, my spouse, with me from Lebanon: look from the top of Amana, from the top of Shenir and Hermon, from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards” (Son 4:8) — a call away from high and dangerous places to be with him. “Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one chain of thy neck” (Son 4:9). “How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse! how much better is thy love than wine!” (Son 4:10). The doubled title my sister, my spouse joins kinship and covenant: she is his by blood-nearness and by promise. The Song is first of all what it appears to be — the marriage of a man and a woman, given by God, praised without embarrassment — and Paul says of that very union that it signifies something further: “This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church” (Eph 5:32). The believer's standing is not that of a servant only. The church is a bride, called by name, delighted in, and told to come.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a spouse as a man or woman engaged or joined in wedlock; a married person, husband or wife; and also a person betrothed.

expand to see more

SPOUSE, n. A man or woman engaged or joined in wedlock; a married person, husband or wife.

2. A person betrothed or promised in marriage.

BRIDE, n. A woman new married, or about to be married.

BETROTH', v.t. To contract to any one, in order to a future marriage; to promise or pledge in marriage.

Key Scripture

Song of Solomon 4:9 — "Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one chain of thy neck."

Song of Solomon 4:10 — "How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse! how much better is thy love than wine! and the smell of thine ointments than all spices!"

Song of Solomon 4:8 — "Come with me from Lebanon, my spouse, with me from Lebanon: look from the top of Amana, from the top of Shenir and Hermon, from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards."

Ephesians 5:32 — "This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church."

Modern Corruption

Marriage is redefined as a contract of two consenting parties on any terms, and the Song is either allegorized until nothing bodily remains or read as though it were nothing else.

expand to see more

Ephesians 5:32 makes marriage a sign, and a sign cannot be redefined by the parties who use it. Paul says the union of one man and one woman is a great mystery concerning Christ and the church; therefore its shape — one husband, one wife, covenanted for life, ordered in headship and in love — is not a social arrangement subject to revision but a picture God is using. To alter the picture is not to expand a human institution; it is to falsify a statement about Christ. That is why the church cannot treat the definition of marriage as a secondary matter, however costly it becomes to say so.

Two opposite errors have also plagued the reading of the Song itself. One allegorizes it so thoroughly that the woman disappears and every embrace becomes a doctrine, which cannot be right, since God gave the book its plain sense first and blessed the marriage bed without apology. The other refuses any further reference at all, which leaves the church without the Old Testament's richest vocabulary for the love of Christ toward His people — and Scripture itself will not allow it, since the prophets call the LORD Israel's husband and John sees the marriage supper of the Lamb. The Song is a real marriage, and a real marriage is a sign.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kallah (H3618), bride, spouse, daughter-in-law — Song of Solomon 4:8-12, 5:1, Jeremiah 2:32; Greek numphe (G3565), a bride, in Revelation 21:9.

expand to see more

Hebrew kallah (H3618) — bride, spouse; Song of Solomon 4:8-12 and 5:1, Jeremiah 2:32, Hosea 4:13.

Hebrew achoti kallah — my sister, my spouse; the doubled title joining kinship and covenant.

Greek numphe (G3565) — a bride; Revelation 21:9, John 3:29 of the bridegroom's friend.

Greek musterion (G3466) — a mystery, something once hidden and now revealed; Ephesians 5:32.

Latin sponsa, from spondere, to promise solemnly — the English word carries the vow in its root.

Usage

"“My sister, my spouse” — kinship and covenant in one title."

"“Come with me from Lebanon… from the lions' dens” — called away, and to him."

"“I speak concerning Christ and the church” — the marriage is a sign."
